title: LaRA: Large Rank Adaptation for Speech and Text Cross-Modal Learning in Large Language Models

reviews.summary: The paper introduces a method for adapting (fine-tuning) a pre-trained text-only LLM and turn it into a text-and-speech language model (speech being represented by HuBERT discrete units). The method relies on what the authors call "LaRA", which can be described as LoRA with a larger ("low") rank than generally used. They claim to show that lower ranks (as generally used in LoRA) are insufficient for the model to correctly adapt to the addition of the speech modality, whereas their higher rank adapters help.
reviews.strengths:
- Interesting idea implemented in a sound way
- Experiments carefully described and analysed (I particularly appreciated the brief discussion in Section 5.1 and Figure 5)
reviews.weaknesses:
- The paper is not always very clearly written (see the next section for specific comments)
- The state of the art seems incomplete (and at times inaccurate, see the next section). In particular, the authors could have cited (C. Wang et al. 2023) [Vall-E], (Hassid et al. 2023) [who showed that fine-tuning pre-trained text-only LMs can lead to improving speech LM performance], (T. Wang et al. 2023) [VioLA; similar to AudioPALM, cited by the authors), (Nachmani et al. 2023) [Spectron; similar to SpeechGPT, cited by the authors), (Fathullah et al. 2023), (Chou et al. 2023) [SUTLM], (Haiti et al. 2023) [VoxtLM] and (Nguyen et al. 2024) [SPIRIT-LM], amongst others.
- The authors advocate for adapting the pre-trained model by making trainable as many as 27% of all parameters. This is a lot, and would be more convincing if a comparison with standard fine-tuning was provided.
reviews.questions:
The paper should be proof-read by a native English speaker. Here are a few suggestions:
- the paper by the "Gemini Team" should not be cited as "Team et al. 2024) (line 034)
- "the to" on line 045 should be fixed
- the citation for the LauraGPT arXiv paper seems incorrect to me. This paper exists in four versions (v1 to v4). Versions v1 to v3 have Jiaming Wang as a first author, version v4 has Zhihao Du as a first author. The submission cites the paper as "(Chen et al. 2023)", which is probably incorrect.
- variables are not always clearly defined. For instance: is uppercase variable "K" on line 222 the same as the lowercase "k" on line 199? And on line 237? And on line 384? Is it also the same as "k" on line 286?
- in Table 3, the column entitled "Trainable-Params" (there should be no hyphens) must probably be understood as a number of *billions* of parameters. This should be clarified.

Also, will the source code be released?

reviews.summary: The paper applies LoRA to adapt an LLM to speech and realizes that much larger ranks are required for effective speech adaptation. Hence it calls its method LaRA: Large Rank Adaptation for speech, text cross-modal learning. It first introduces a data modeling framework of concatenating speech and its transcription from the Librispeech-360 and Daily Talk datasets. And then it introduces a fine-tuning framework tying an LLM with a speech tokenizer, and using LoRA adapters for the attention weights of the LLM. This way the training parameters are minimized, since only the adapter weights need to be learnt. It picks Llama-2 7B as its LLM baseline, and HuBERT models as choices for speech tokenization and initializing the speech embedding matrix. It finetunes the Llama-2-LaRA models and observes the validation loss decrease with the increasing rank sizes. The paper also visualizes the speech and text embeddings using t-SNE before and after training to illustrate the closeness of the learned speech, text embeddings.
reviews.strengths:
1) The paper proposes a new framework using LoRA to adapt a text-only LLM to speech with HuBERT as the speech tokenizer.
2) The observation of the model’s performance improving with larger ranks, and the conclusion that cross-modal adaptation requires significantly larger ranks as compared to the same modality is very valuable to the research community.
3) The t-SNE visualization of the embeddings being closer after training illustrates the cross-model adaptability of its method.
reviews.weaknesses:
1) The paper does not provide other strong baselines as alternatives to their LaRA method for cross-modal adaptability. Even if the trainable parameters are higher, it would be good to get a sense to see the results of a model with the traditional adapters as an example, since those extra parameters could still improve the performance of the speech-text LLM. I would point the authors to section 5.1 of the LoRA paper (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2106.09685) which provides a number of strong baselines to compare their method against. Without this comparison, we will not get a sense of how effective the LaRA method is. Also, it would be nice to see the numbers even beyond a rank size of 2048, since the model performance keeps improving and hasn’t saturated yet, with increasing rank size.
2) The paper does not analyze how cross-modal adaptation affects the text-only performance. A simple way to evaluate this could be to compare the Llama-2 7B baseline model’s performance on a text-only version of the valid & test sets with their Llama-2-LaRA models, and see if the text generation capability has worsened. Better would be to simply evaluate all the Llama-2-LaRA models on MMLU as well, comparing the numbers with the Llama-2 7B baseline’s number.
3) The lack of justification for the choice of its data modeling framework, and lack of experimentation in that sense. The paper seems to have the speech tokens followed by the text transcription tokens of the same speech. Would be nice if the paper explicitly mentions if this is the case. This reduces variance in the dataset, as a start, what if we have a set of the speech tokens together and text tokens together and shuffle them. Basically instead of  <speech_A> <text_transcription_A> <speech_B> <text_transcription_B> <speech_C> <text_transcription_C> we can have <speech_A> <speech_B> <text_transcription_C> <speech_C> <text_transcription_A> <text_transcription_B>. In my opinion, the current data modeling framework limits the generalizability of the fine-tuned model.
reviews.questions:
1) Figure 6, b): It seems like the validation and training loss keeps decreasing for the km-1000 model, why stop the training then? I’m assuming the end of the curve signals a stoppage of training. Could you mention your stopping criteria?
2_ Section 3.2: Why initialize from a Gaussian if you’re anyway replacing it with HuBERT’s hidden layer?
3) Table 2: What is psi = alpha / rank? Can you explain, what is this psi?
4) Figure 4: Can you elaborate more on the lack of saturation of loss while increasing the ranks? How does your training converge then?
5) Table 3: Trainable-Params in Millions of Billions, could you explicitly mention? And these results are for the 1000 cluster HuBERT tokenizer?
6) The data modeling framework with the most capability seems to be that of interleaving speech and text tokens together, as employed by the Spirit-LM work (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2402.05755). Would be nice if the authors experimented more in this direction.
7) The paper does not speak about the actual speech generation or speech understanding capability of their model, which would be nice to have, and at least compare it with the HUBERT models used, for ASR as an example.
8) Typos/Nits:
- Section 1: “the to” -> “them to”
- Section 2: Llama 13B, which version of Llama?
- Section 2: “include the” -> “including the”
- Section 2: Llama LLM, which version(s)?
- Section 2: Llama-2, which size(s)
- Section 2: “From the literature we observe that on text-based LLMs”, this sentence doesn’t make sense.
- Section 5: “y_hat_i” -> subscript is needed for i
